decks.title: Magnetism and Matter — Part 1: Bar magnets, magnetic dipoles and flux
goals: Compare a bar magnet with its equivalent solenoid, and magnetic field lines with electric field lines
Use the end-on and broadside-on formulae for the field of a magnet, and find the torque on a magnet in a uniform field
Calculate magnetic flux and convert between tesla, weber per square metre and gauss

slides.heading: Magnetism and Matter
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the bar magnet as a magnetic dipole: its field lines, its field at a point, the torque on it, and magnetic flux.

visual.alt: Field lines of a bar magnet

slides.narration: A compass needle, a fridge magnet and the coil of a motor all behave in the same way: each is a magnetic dipole. In this part we look at the field lines of a bar magnet and see why it acts just like a solenoid, compare its lines with those of an electric dipole, use formulae for its field at a point, find the torque on it, and define magnetic flux.

slides.heading: The bar magnet and its field lines
slides.body_md: Field lines of a bar magnet, traced with a small compass or iron filings:
bullets: Outside the magnet they run from the **N** pole round to the **S** pole; **inside** they continue from S to N.
Every line is a **closed loop**; lines never cross.
The **magnetic moment** $\vec m$ points from S to N inside the magnet (unit A m²).
Breaking a magnet gives two complete magnets: no isolated pole (**monopole**) has ever been found.

visual.alt: Field lines of a bar magnet

slides.narration: Sprinkle iron filings round a bar magnet and they trace curved lines from the north pole round to the south pole. The lines do not stop at the poles: they carry on through the body of the magnet from south to north, so every line is a closed loop. The magnetic moment of the magnet points the same way as the lines inside it, from the south pole to the north pole.

slides.heading: A bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
slides.body_md:
A short solenoid carrying a current has **the same field pattern** as a bar magnet: the end where the current is anticlockwise as seen from outside acts as N. Its moment is
$$m = NIA$$
bullets: In a magnet, the electrons of each atom act as tiny **current loops**; in a magnet they are aligned, so their effects add like the turns of a solenoid.
Inside currents of neighbouring loops cancel, leaving a net current round the surface: an equivalent solenoid.

visual.alt: Field lines of the equivalent solenoid

slides.narration: Now compare a short solenoid carrying a current. Outside it, the field lines are exactly those of the bar magnet, and inside they run along the axis. The reason is that every atom of a magnet contains circulating electrons, tiny current loops. In a magnet these loops are lined up, so the magnet behaves like a solenoid whose moment is the number of turns times the current times the area.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: an equivalent solenoid
slides.body_md: A bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 0.90 A m². It is to be replaced by a solenoid of 500 turns, each of radius 1.2 cm. What current is needed?
bullets: Area of a turn: $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.012)^2 \approx 4.52 \times 10^{-4}$ m².
$I = \dfrac{m}{NA} = \dfrac{0.90}{500 \times 4.52 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 3.98$ A, about 4 A.
The end towards which the moment points (current anticlockwise as seen from outside) takes the place of the N pole.

visual.alt: Field lines of the equivalent solenoid

slides.narration: Each turn has an area of pi times one point two centimetres squared, about four point five square centimetres. Five hundred turns of that area need a current of nought point nine divided by five hundred times the area, close to four amperes, to match the magnet. The end of the solenoid where the current circulates anticlockwise, as you look at it from outside, takes the place of the north pole.

slides.heading: Magnetic and electric field lines compared
slides.body_md: Both dipoles have the same pattern **far away**, but close up they differ:
bullets: Electric lines **start on +q and end on −q**; magnetic lines have **no ends**.
Between the charges $\vec E$ points **opposite** to $\vec p$; inside the magnet $\vec B$ points **along** $\vec m$.
Hence the net magnetic flux through **any closed surface is zero**, while the electric flux through a surface round a charge is not.

visual.alt: Electric dipole and bar magnet field lines compared

slides.narration: Put an electric dipole beside a bar magnet. Far away their field lines look alike. Close up there is a real difference. Electric lines begin on the positive charge and end on the negative one, and between the charges the field points opposite to the dipole moment. Magnetic lines never end: they run straight through the magnet, along its moment. This happens because there are no magnetic charges.

slides.heading: Field of a magnetic dipole: end-on and broadside-on
slides.body_md:
For a magnet of magnetic length $2l$ and moment $m$, at distance $d$ from its centre (formulae only; derivations are not required):
$$B_\text{end-on} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2md}{(d^2 - l^2)^2}, \qquad B_\text{broadside-on} = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2}}$$
bullets: End-on (on the axis): $\vec B$ along $\vec m$. Broadside-on (on the perpendicular bisector): $\vec B$ opposite to $\vec m$.
Short magnet, $d \gg l$: $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{d^3}$ end-on and $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{d^3}$ broadside-on, with $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}$ T m A$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: Two positions matter. End-on means a point on the axis of the magnet; broadside-on means a point on the line that cuts the magnet at right angles through its centre. On the axis the field points along the moment; on the bisector it points the opposite way. For a short magnet, far away, the end-on field is two m over d cubed and the broadside-on field m over d cubed, times mu nought over four pi.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a magnet that is not short
slides.body_md: A bar magnet of magnetic length 5.0 cm has a moment of 0.40 A m². Find the field 10 cm from its centre (a) end-on, (b) broadside-on, and compare with the short-magnet formulae.
bullets: Short-magnet values: $8.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T and $4.0 \times 10^{-5}$ T. The ratio is no longer 2, because $l$ is a quarter of $d$.

visual.alt: Table of worked example 2: for a 5 centimetre magnet of moment 0.40 ampere square metre at 10 centimetres, the end-on field is about 9.1 times ten to the minus five tesla against 8.0 from the short-magnet formula, and the broadside-on field about 3.65 against 4.0

slides.narration: Here half the length is two and a half centimetres and the distance is ten. End-on, the field works out at about nine point one times ten to the minus five tesla; broadside-on, about three point six five times ten to the minus five. The short-magnet formulae would give eight and four, a little low and a little high. When the magnet is not much shorter than the distance, use the full formulae.

slides.heading: How the field falls with distance
slides.body_md:
For a short magnet both fields fall as $1/d^3$, much faster than the $1/d^2$ field of a point charge. At the same distance:
$$\dfrac{B_\text{end-on}}{B_\text{broadside-on}} = 2$$
bullets: Doubling $d$ divides either field by $2^3 = 8$.
To compare two points, write both fields in terms of $m$ and the distances, then divide.

visual.alt: Field of a short bar magnet against distance from its centre: both curves fall as the inverse cube of distance, the end-on curve always twice the broadside-on curve at the same distance
visual.caption: Doubling d divides either field by 8.

slides.narration: The graph shows both fields of a short magnet against distance. Each falls as the inverse cube of the distance, so moving twice as far away cuts the field to an eighth. At every distance the end-on curve is exactly twice the broadside-on curve. To compare the field at two different points, write each in terms of the moment and its own distance, and divide one by the other.

slides.heading: Torque on a magnetic dipole
slides.body_md:
A magnet of moment $\vec m$ in a uniform field $\vec B$ feels **no net force** but a **torque**
$$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B, \qquad \tau = mB\sin\theta$$
which turns $\vec m$ towards $\vec B$ (the same law as for a current loop, chapter 8).
bullets: $\theta = 0^\circ$: zero torque, **stable**; $\theta = 180^\circ$: zero torque, **unstable**; $\theta = 90^\circ$: largest torque $mB$.

slides.narration: A magnet in a uniform field is just like the current loop of the last chapter. There is no net force, but there is a turning effect, m cross B, of size m B sine theta. It always tries to swing the moment round into line with the field. Lined up with the field, the magnet is stable; pointing exactly against it, the torque is also zero, but the slightest nudge makes it turn right round.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: torque on a suspended magnet
slides.body_md: A magnet of moment 0.60 A m² hangs so that it can turn in a horizontal plane, in a uniform horizontal field of 0.025 T. Find the torque on it when its axis is (a) at right angles to the field, (b) at 30° to the field, and say which way it turns.
bullets: (a) $\tau = mB = 0.60 \times 0.025 = 0.015$ N m (the largest possible).
(b) $\tau = mB\sin 30^\circ = 0.015 \times 0.5 = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
In both cases the torque turns the magnet so that its moment swings towards the field.

headers: Angle θ between m and B

visual.alt: Table of the torque on a magnet at three orientations: zero and stable at 0 degrees, largest at 90 degrees, zero and unstable at 180 degrees

slides.narration: At right angles to the field, the torque is simply m times B: nought point six times nought point nought two five, which is nought point nought one five newton metre. At thirty degrees the sine is one half, so the torque halves to seven point five times ten to the minus three newton metre. Either way the magnet turns to bring its moment into line with the field.

slides.heading: Magnetic flux
slides.body_md:
The **magnetic flux** through a flat surface of area $A$ in a uniform field is
$$\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A = BA\cos\theta$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec B$ and the **normal** to the surface. Flux is a **scalar**; it measures how many field lines cross the surface.
bullets: Greatest, $BA$, when the surface faces the field; zero when the field runs along the surface.
Through any **closed** surface the net magnetic flux is zero.

slides.narration: Magnetic flux tells us how much field passes through a surface. For a flat surface it is the field times the area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the normal. Facing the field squarely, the surface catches the most lines. Tilted, it catches fewer: at sixty degrees, only half. With the field running along the surface, none cross it, and the flux is zero.

slides.heading: Flux density and its units
slides.body_md: Since $\Phi = BA$ for a surface facing the field, $B = \Phi/A$: the magnetic field is the **flux density**, the flux per unit area normal to the field.
bullets: Unit of flux: the **weber**, 1 Wb = 1 T m².
Unit of B: the **tesla**, 1 T = 1 Wb m⁻².
The **gauss** is still used: 1 G $= 10^{-4}$ T, so 1 T $= 10^4$ G.

visual.alt: Table of the units of magnetic flux and flux density: the weber, the tesla equal to a weber per square metre, and the gauss equal to ten to the minus four tesla, with typical values

slides.narration: Turning the formula round, the field is the flux through each square metre held at right angles to it, which is why B is also called the flux density. Flux is measured in webers, and one tesla is one weber per square metre. An older unit, the gauss, is still common: one gauss is ten to the minus four tesla. The Earth’s field is about half a gauss.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: flux through a square loop
slides.body_md: A square loop of side 12 cm is in a uniform field of 0.50 T. Find the flux through it when (a) its plane is perpendicular to the field, (b) its normal makes 60° with the field, (c) its plane is parallel to the field. Express the field in gauss.
bullets: (b) $\Phi = BA\cos 60^\circ = 7.2 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.5 = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb. (c) $\Phi = 0$.

visual.caption: Beyond 90° the field passes through the other face: the flux is negative.

slides.narration: The area is nought point nought one four four square metre. Facing the field, the flux is half a tesla times that area, seven point two milliwebers. With the normal at sixty degrees, the cosine halves it to three point six milliwebers. With the plane along the field, no lines cross, and the flux is zero. Half a tesla is five thousand gauss.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Closed loops; inside S → N, along $\vec m$; no monopoles
$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$; no net force in uniform B
$\Phi = BA\cos\theta$; Wb; 1 T = 1 Wb m⁻² = $10^4$ G

visual.alt: Summary table of field lines, the equivalent solenoid, the end-on and broadside-on fields, the torque on a magnet and magnetic flux

slides.narration: To sum up: a bar magnet behaves like a solenoid, and its field lines are closed loops because there are no magnetic monopoles. On its axis the field points along the moment, and on its bisector against it, half as strong for a short magnet. In a uniform field it feels a torque m cross B but no net force. Flux is B A cos theta, in webers, and a tesla is a weber per square metre.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Say which position (end-on or broadside-on) you are using and give the direction of B with its size.
Use the short-magnet formulae only when the magnet is short compared with d, or when told to.
In τ = mB sin θ and Φ = BA cos θ, check what θ is measured from.
Convert cm to m and gauss to tesla before substituting.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: When you calculate a field, name the position, end-on or broadside-on, and give the direction as well as the size. Use the short-magnet formulae only when the magnet really is short compared with the distance. In the torque and flux formulae, check whether the angle is measured from the field or from the normal. And convert centimetres to metres, and gauss to tesla, before you substitute.

decks.title: Magnetism and Matter — Part 2: Magnetic materials, electromagnets and the B–H loop
goals: Define magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability, and use B = μ₀(H + M)
Classify dia-, para- and ferromagnetic substances and apply Curie’s law and the Curie temperature
Explain electromagnets and the B–H loop, and choose materials for permanent magnets, electromagnets and transformer cores

slides.heading: Magnetic Materials
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what happens to matter placed in a magnetic field, and how we choose materials for magnets and cores.

visual.alt: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetic samples in a uniform field

slides.narration: Every material responds to a magnetic field, though most respond very weakly. In this part we describe that response with a few quantities, sort materials into diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic, see how temperature affects them, and then put ferromagnets to work in electromagnets and transformer cores, using the B H loop to choose the right material for each job.

slides.heading: Magnetisation M and magnetic intensity H
slides.body_md:
**Magnetisation** $M$ is the net magnetic moment per unit volume of a material, $M = m/V$ (A m⁻¹). **Magnetic intensity** $H$ is the part of the field due to the free currents; inside a long solenoid $H = nI$ (A m⁻¹). The total field is
$$B = \mu_0(H + M)$$
bullets: With no material, $M = 0$ and $B = \mu_0 H$.

rows: set by the free currents, e.g. $nI$ in a solenoid

visual.alt: Table of magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability with their meanings and units

slides.narration: When a material sits inside a solenoid, two things make up the field. The current in the windings sets up the magnetic intensity H, equal to n I. The material itself becomes magnetised, and its magnetisation M is its magnetic moment per unit volume. Both are measured in amperes per metre, and the field is mu nought times their sum.

slides.heading: Susceptibility and relative permeability
slides.body_md:
For most materials $M$ is proportional to $H$: $M = \chi H$, where $\chi$ is the **magnetic susceptibility** (no unit). Then
$$B = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H = \mu_0\mu_r H, \qquad \mu_r = 1 + \chi$$
$\mu_r$ is the **relative permeability**; the permeability is $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r$.
bullets: $\chi < 0$: diamagnetic. $\chi$ small and $> 0$: paramagnetic. $\chi \gg 1$: ferromagnetic.

rows: set by the free currents, e.g. $nI$ in a solenoid

visual.alt: Table of magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability with their meanings and units

slides.narration: In most materials the magnetisation is proportional to H. The constant is the susceptibility, chi, a pure number. Putting M equal to chi H into the field equation gives B equals mu nought times one plus chi times H. One plus chi is the relative permeability. The sign and size of the susceptibility tell us at once what kind of material we have.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a solenoid with a core
slides.body_md: A long solenoid with 2400 turns per metre carries 0.50 A. Its core has susceptibility 349. Find $H$, $\mu_r$, $B$ in the core and $M$.
bullets: $B = \mu_0\mu_r H = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 350 \times 1200 \approx 0.528$ T.

rows: set by the free currents, e.g. $nI$ in a solenoid

visual.alt: Table of magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability with their meanings and units

slides.narration: The windings give H equal to twenty four hundred times half an ampere, twelve hundred amperes per metre. The relative permeability is three hundred and fifty, so the field in the core is about nought point five three tesla, three hundred and fifty times what the empty coil would give. The magnetisation is the susceptibility times H, about four point two times ten to the five amperes per metre.

slides.heading: Three kinds of magnetic material
slides.body_md: Field lines through a sample placed in a uniform field:
bullets: **Diamagnetic** ($\chi < 0$): lines spread out slightly; $B$ inside a little less.
**Paramagnetic** ($\chi$ small, $> 0$): lines crowd in slightly.
**Ferromagnetic** ($\chi \gg 1$): lines are drawn strongly into the sample.

visual.alt: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetic samples in a uniform field

slides.narration: Place three samples in the same uniform field. In a diamagnetic sample the field lines spread out a little, so the field inside is slightly weaker. In a paramagnetic sample they crowd in slightly. In a ferromagnetic sample they are drawn in very strongly. The drawing exaggerates the first two effects: real diamagnets and paramagnets change the field by only a few parts in a hundred thousand.

slides.heading: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism compared
slides.body_md: The difference lies in the atoms:
columns:
**Diamagnetic and paramagnetic**
- Dia: no permanent atomic moment; the field induces small moments that oppose it, so the sample moves towards weaker field
- Para: permanent moments, partly lined up by the field, so the sample moves towards stronger field

**Ferromagnetic**
- Permanent moments lined up spontaneously in small regions called domains
- A modest field reorients whole domains: very large M
- Stays magnetised after the field is removed

visual.alt: Table comparing diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances by atomic moments, susceptibility, relative permeability, behaviour in a non-uniform field, effect of temperature and examples

slides.narration: Diamagnetism is present in every atom: an applied field alters the electrons’ orbits so that they produce small moments opposing it. Paramagnetic atoms carry permanent moments, which the field partly lines up against the jostling of thermal motion. In ferromagnets the moments line up by themselves within domains, so even a small field produces a huge magnetisation, and some of it remains when the field is removed.

slides.heading: Quick check: a small negative susceptibility
slides.body_md: Choose the correct option.

visual.alt: Dia-, para- and ferromagnetic samples in a uniform field

slides.narration: Think about the sign of the susceptibility.

slides.heading: Curie’s law for paramagnets
slides.body_md:
The susceptibility of a paramagnet falls as the temperature rises:
$$\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$$
($T$ in kelvin; $C$ is the Curie constant of the material). Thermal agitation disorders the permanent moments that the field tries to line up.
bullets: At fixed $H$, $M = \chi H \propto 1/T$ (well below saturation).
Diamagnetic susceptibility hardly depends on temperature.

visual.alt: Susceptibility of the paramagnetic salt of worked example 6 against absolute temperature: a hyperbola, 8 times ten to the minus four at 140 kelvin, 5.6 at 200 kelvin and 3.5 at 320 kelvin
visual.caption: Curie’s law: χT stays constant.

slides.narration: For a paramagnet, heat works against the field. The hotter the sample, the more violently its atoms jostle, and the harder it is for the field to line up their moments. Curie found that the susceptibility is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature: chi equals C over T. Halve the temperature in kelvin and the susceptibility doubles. Diamagnetism, by contrast, is almost unaffected by temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: Curie’s law
slides.body_md: A paramagnetic salt has susceptibility $5.6 \times 10^{-4}$ at 200 K. Find (a) its Curie constant, (b) its susceptibility at 320 K, (c) the temperature at which its susceptibility is $8.0 \times 10^{-4}$.

visual.alt: Susceptibility of the paramagnetic salt of worked example 6 against absolute temperature: a hyperbola, 8 times ten to the minus four at 140 kelvin, 5.6 at 200 kelvin and 3.5 at 320 kelvin
visual.caption: Curie’s law: χT stays constant.

slides.narration: The product of susceptibility and temperature is the Curie constant: five point six times ten to the minus four times two hundred gives nought point one one two kelvin. At three hundred and twenty kelvin, divide the constant by the temperature: three point five times ten to the minus four. For eight times ten to the minus four, divide the constant by that value: one hundred and forty kelvin.

slides.heading: Ferromagnetism: domains and the Curie temperature
slides.body_md: A ferromagnet is made of **domains**, each spontaneously magnetised. With no field they point in random directions. A weak field makes favourably aligned domains **grow**; a strong field **rotates** the rest until the sample is **saturated**.
bullets: Above the **Curie temperature** $T_C$ thermal agitation destroys the alignment within domains: the material becomes **paramagnetic**.
On cooling below $T_C$ the domains form again.

slides.heading: Electromagnets
slides.body_md:
An **electromagnet** is a coil wound on a **soft-iron** core. The core multiplies the field of the coil by its relative permeability:
$$B \approx \mu_0\mu_r nI$$
bullets: Strength rises with the **turns per unit length** $n$, the **current** $I$ and the **permeability** of the core; a U-shaped core with a small air gap helps too.
Above a certain current the core **saturates**; then extra current adds little.
Switch off the current and soft iron loses its magnetism: used in cranes, relays, bells and door locks.

On its own, the coil gives just under a millitesla. The iron core multiplies this by fourteen hundred, to about one point three two tesla, provided the iron has not reached saturation.

slides.heading: The B–H loop: hysteresis
slides.body_md: Take a ferromagnet through a full cycle of $H$ and plot $B$ (qualitatively):
bullets: **Saturation:** B levels off when the domains are all aligned.
**Retentivity** (remanence): the $B$ left when $H$ is brought back to zero.
**Coercivity:** the reverse $H$ needed to bring $B$ to zero.
B **lags** behind H (hysteresis); the loop area measures the energy turned into heat each cycle.

visual.alt: The B–H (hysteresis) loop of a ferromagnet

slides.narration: Increase H from zero and B climbs until it levels off at saturation. Now reduce H to zero: B does not return to zero, because the domains stay partly aligned. What is left is the retentivity. To remove it we must apply a reverse H, the coercivity. Going on round the cycle traces a closed loop. B always lags behind H, and the area of the loop measures the energy wasted as heat in each cycle.

slides.heading: Soft iron and steel compared
slides.body_md: The loops of two ferromagnets:
bullets: **Soft iron:** narrow loop: **low coercivity**, high permeability, slightly higher retentivity, **small loop area** (little energy lost).
**Steel:** wide loop: **high coercivity**, so its magnetisation is hard to destroy; large loop area.

visual.alt: B–H loops of soft iron and steel
visual.caption: Qualitative: real coercivities differ by a factor of a thousand or more.

slides.narration: Compare the loops of soft iron and steel. Soft iron gives a tall, narrow loop: it is easily magnetised, its coercivity is small, and little energy is lost in each cycle, though it keeps a fair retentivity while no reverse field acts. Steel gives a wide loop: once magnetised, it needs a large reverse field to demagnetise it, which is exactly what a permanent magnet needs.

slides.heading: Choosing magnetic materials
slides.body_md: Match the material to the job:
bullets: **Permanent magnets:** high retentivity **and** high coercivity, e.g. steel, alnico, ferrites.
**Electromagnet cores:** high permeability, low retentivity and low coercivity, e.g. soft iron.
**Transformer cores** (230 V, 50 Hz mains): high permeability and a **narrow loop** to keep the hysteresis loss small, e.g. laminated soft iron or silicon steel.

rows: high permeability, low retentivity, low coercivity
high permeability, low coercivity, narrow loop (small loss)
soft iron or silicon steel, laminated

visual.alt: Table of the choice of magnetic materials: permanent magnets need high retentivity and coercivity, as in steel or alnico; electromagnet cores need high permeability and low retentivity and coercivity, as in soft iron; transformer cores need high permeability and a narrow loop, as in laminated soft iron or silicon steel

slides.narration: A permanent magnet must keep its magnetism against knocks and stray fields, so it needs both a high retentivity and a high coercivity: steel or alnico. An electromagnet must switch off cleanly, so its core needs a low retentivity and coercivity: soft iron. A transformer core goes round its loop fifty times a second, so it needs a narrow loop and a high permeability: laminated soft iron or silicon steel.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:
bullets: $B = \mu_0(H + M)$, $M = \chi H$, $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$.
Paramagnets: $\chi = C/T$. Ferromagnets become paramagnetic above $T_C$.
Electromagnet: $B \approx \mu_0\mu_r nI$ up to saturation.
B–H loop: retentivity, coercivity; choose hard (wide-loop) materials for permanent magnets, soft (narrow-loop) ones for cores.

visual.alt: Table comparing diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances by atomic moments, susceptibility, relative permeability, behaviour in a non-uniform field, effect of temperature and examples

slides.narration: To sum up: the field in a material is mu nought times H plus M, and the relative permeability is one plus the susceptibility. Diamagnets have a small negative susceptibility, paramagnets a small positive one that follows Curie’s law, and ferromagnets a huge one that vanishes above the Curie temperature. Wide B H loops suit permanent magnets; narrow ones suit electromagnet and transformer cores.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Classify from the sign and size of χ, or from μr compared with 1.
In Curie’s law always use kelvin.
For a material in a solenoid: H = nI first, then B = μ₀μrH and M = χH.
When choosing materials, name the property (retentivity, coercivity, permeability, loop area) and say why it matters for that use.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Classify a material from the sign and size of its susceptibility, or from whether its relative permeability is above or below one. Always use kelvin in Curie’s law. For a material inside a solenoid, find H from the current first, then B and M. And when you choose a material, name the property that matters, such as coercivity or loop area, and say why it suits that use.

sections.heading: 1. The bar magnet, its equivalent solenoid and its field lines
sections.body_md:
- Field lines of a bar magnet run from N to S **outside** and from S to N **inside**: every line is a **closed loop**; lines never cross. The magnetic moment $\vec m$ points from S to N (A m²).
- A current-carrying **solenoid** has the same field pattern: it is the **equivalent solenoid** of the magnet, with $m = NIA$. In a magnet, aligned atomic current loops act like the turns of the solenoid.
- **Electric lines** start on +q and end on −q, and between the charges $\vec E$ is opposite to $\vec p$; **magnetic lines** have no ends and inside the magnet $\vec B$ is along $\vec m$. No **magnetic monopole** has been found, so the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.

key_terms.definition_md: A hypothetical isolated north or south pole; none has been observed, so magnetic field lines have no ends.
A current-carrying solenoid whose field pattern and moment NIA match those of a given bar magnet.

sections.heading: 2. Field of a magnetic dipole; torque on a magnet
sections.body_md:
- Magnet of magnetic length 2l, moment m, point at distance d from its centre (formulae only; derivations not required):
  - **end-on** (on the axis): $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2md}{(d^2 - l^2)^2}$, **along** $\vec m$;
  - **broadside-on** (on the perpendicular bisector): $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2}}$, **opposite** to $\vec m$.
- **Short magnet** ($d \gg l$): $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{d^3}$ and $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{d^3}$; both $\propto 1/d^3$; end-on is twice broadside-on at the same d. $\mu_0/4\pi = 10^{-7}$ T m A⁻¹.
- In a **uniform** field: no net force, torque $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$, $\tau = mB\sin\theta$; stable at θ = 0°, unstable at θ = 180°, largest (mB) at 90°.

key_terms.definition_md: A point on the axis of the magnet, produced; the field there points along m.
A point on the perpendicular bisector of the magnet; the field there points opposite to m.

sections.heading: 3. Magnetic flux and flux density
sections.body_md:
- **Magnetic flux** through a flat surface in a uniform field: $\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A = BA\cos\theta$, θ between $\vec B$ and the **normal**. A scalar; unit **weber** (1 Wb = 1 T m²).
- Largest ($BA$) when the surface faces the field; zero when the field lies along the surface; negative when B passes through the other face.
- $B = \Phi/A$ is the **flux density**: unit **tesla**, 1 T = 1 Wb m⁻². **Gauss**: 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T. Earth’s field is about 0.5 G; a strong laboratory magnet about 1 T.

key_terms.definition_md: The scalar product of B with the area vector of a surface, BA cos θ; unit weber.
A non-SI unit of magnetic field: 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T.

sections.heading: 4. Magnetic properties of materials
sections.body_md:
- **Magnetisation** $M = m/V$ (A m⁻¹); **magnetic intensity** $H$ (A m⁻¹), $H = nI$ in a long solenoid; $B = \mu_0(H + M)$.
- **Susceptibility** $\chi = M/H$ (no unit); **relative permeability** $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$; $B = \mu_0\mu_r H$; permeability $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r$.
- **Diamagnetic:** χ small, negative, μr slightly < 1; induced moments oppose the field; pushed towards weaker field; almost independent of temperature (bismuth, copper, water).
- **Paramagnetic:** χ small, positive, μr slightly > 1; permanent moments partly aligned; pulled towards stronger field; **Curie’s law** $\chi = C/T$ (aluminium, sodium, oxygen).
- **Ferromagnetic:** χ and μr very large; moments aligned in **domains**; above the **Curie temperature** $T_C$ it becomes paramagnetic (iron about 1043 K, nickel about 631 K, gadolinium about 293 K).

key_terms.definition_md: Ratio M/H of the magnetisation of a material to the magnetic intensity; negative for diamagnets.
The temperature above which a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic, because thermal agitation destroys the alignment within its domains.
A small region of a ferromagnet in which the atomic moments are spontaneously aligned.

sections.heading: 5. Electromagnets, the B–H loop and the choice of materials
sections.body_md:
- **Electromagnet:** a coil on a soft-iron core, $B \approx \mu_0\mu_r nI$; stronger with more turns per unit length, more current and a core of higher permeability (and a small air gap), until the core **saturates**.
- **B–H loop** (qualitative): B rises to **saturation**; at H = 0 a field B, the **retentivity**, remains; a reverse H, the **coercivity**, is needed to make B zero. B lags behind H (**hysteresis**); the loop area measures the energy lost as heat per cycle.
- **Soft iron:** narrow loop, low coercivity, high permeability, slightly higher retentivity than steel. **Steel:** wide loop, high coercivity.
- **Choice:** permanent magnets — high retentivity and high coercivity (steel, alnico); electromagnet cores — high permeability, low retentivity and coercivity (soft iron); transformer cores — high permeability, narrow loop (laminated soft iron, silicon steel).

Sign and size of χ for a diamagnet?
Curie’s law?
cards.back_md: $\chi = C/T$ for a paramagnet, T in kelvin.

cards.front_md: What happens to a ferromagnet above its Curie temperature?
cards.back_md: Its domains break up and it becomes paramagnetic.

cards.front_md: Field in an electromagnet core?
Retentivity?

questions.stem_md: An electric dipole (charges +q and −q) and a short bar magnet are drawn side by side, with the dipole moment p and the magnetic moment m both pointing to the right. At the centre of each — midway between the two charges, and in the middle of the magnet itself — the field points

options.text_md: to the right in both
to the left in both
to the left between the charges, but to the right inside the magnet
to the right between the charges, but to the left inside the magnet

questions.solution_md: p points from −q to +q, and between the charges E runs from +q to −q: to the left, opposite to p. The magnetic lines are closed loops that run through the magnet from S to N: to the right, along m. This is the clearest difference between the two patterns — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** However a closed surface is drawn near a bar magnet — even one that cuts through the body of the magnet — the total magnetic flux out of it is zero.

**Reason (R):** Magnetic field lines have no starting or finishing points, so every line that leaves a closed surface must cross back into it somewhere.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: with no monopoles the lines are closed loops, so the outward and inward crossings of any closed surface cancel — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Within the body of a bar magnet, its field lines are directed from the north pole towards the south pole.

**Reason (R):** Outside a bar magnet the field lines run from its north pole round to its south pole, and every line is a closed loop.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: because the loops are closed and run N → S outside, they must return S → N inside the magnet, along its magnetic moment — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A long solenoid behaves like a bar magnet; if the battery connections are swapped so that the current flows the other way round the turns, the end that was a north pole becomes a south pole.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Reversing the current reverses the magnetic moment NIA (right-hand rule), so the polarities of the two ends are exchanged.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 1.8 A m² is to be replaced by an equivalent solenoid of 600 turns, each turn enclosing 5.0 cm². What current must the solenoid carry, in amperes?
questions.solution_md: $m = NIA$, so $I = \dfrac{m}{NA} = \dfrac{1.8}{600 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{1.8}{0.30} = 6.0$ A.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between the field lines of a bar magnet and those of an electric dipole, and give the physical reason for the first.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Magnetic lines form **closed loops**, running N → S outside the magnet and S → N inside; electric lines **start on +q and end on −q**. Reason: no **magnetic monopoles** exist, so a magnetic line has nowhere to begin or end. (ii) Inside the magnet B points **along m**; between the charges E points **opposite to p**.

questions.solution_md: Closed loops versus lines ending on charges; direction inside.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a bar magnet can be treated as an equivalent solenoid. A bar magnet 8.0 cm long has a magnetic moment of 2.4 A m². It is to be replaced by a solenoid of the same length with 400 turns of radius 1.5 cm. What current is needed, and which end of the solenoid must act as its north pole?

answer.model_answer_md: Each atom of the magnet behaves as a tiny current loop; in a magnet these loops are aligned, so their currents cancel inside and leave a net current circulating round the surface, exactly like the turns of a solenoid. Both give the same closed field-line pattern and a moment along the axis. For the solenoid $m = NI\pi r^2$, so $I = \dfrac{m}{N\pi r^2} = \dfrac{2.4}{400 \times \pi \times (0.015)^2} \approx 8.49$ A. The end that the moment points towards, where the current is anticlockwise as seen from outside, must take the place of the magnet's north pole.

questions.solution_md: Aligned atomic current loops; m = NIπr².

marking_scheme.step: Aligned atomic current loops act like solenoid turns; same field pattern
N end: the end m points to (anticlockwise current seen from outside)

questions.stem_md: A thin, uniformly magnetised steel strip of magnetic moment m is bent at its midpoint so that its two halves are at right angles, each half keeping its magnetisation along its own length. The magnetic moment of the bent strip is

options.text_md: m

questions.solution_md: Each half is a dipole of moment $m/2$ along its own length. The two moments are perpendicular, so the resultant is $\sqrt{(m/2)^2 + (m/2)^2} = m/\sqrt2$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Snapping a bar magnet in two always gives two complete magnets; a particle carrying only a north pole or only a south pole, never yet detected, is called a magnetic ___.
questions.solution_md: A magnetic **monopole**. Because none exists, magnetic field lines have no ends.

questions.stem_md: A short bar magnet has a magnetic moment of 2.5 A m². Find the magnetic field it produces at an end-on point 25 cm from its centre, in μT.
questions.solution_md: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{d^3} = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{2 \times 2.5}{(0.25)^3} = 3.2 \times 10^{-5}$ T, i.e. $3.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{6} = 32$ μT, along the magnetic moment.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of magnetic length 10 cm has a magnetic moment of 1.2 A m². Using the broadside-on formula for a magnet of finite length, find the field at a point on its perpendicular bisector 12 cm from its centre, in μT (3 significant figures).

A bar magnet of magnetic length 6.0 cm and magnetic moment 0.80 A m² lies along a straight line. Using the end-on formula for a magnet of finite length, find the field on this line 9.0 cm from the centre of the magnet, in μT (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $l = 0.030$ m and $d = 0.090$ m: $d^2 - l^2 = 0.0081 - 0.0009 = 0.0072$ m². $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2md}{(d^2 - l^2)^2} \approx 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{2 \times 0.80 \times 0.090}{(0.0072)^2} \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-4}$ T, i.e. $2.78 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{6} = 278$ μT, along the magnetic moment.

marking_scheme.step: d² − l² = 0.0072 m² in the end-on formula

questions.stem_md: Point P lies end-on to a short bar magnet, 20 cm from its centre, and point Q lies broadside-on to the same magnet, 10 cm from its centre. The ratio of the field strengths $B_P : B_Q$ is
questions.solution_md: $B_P = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{(0.20)^3}$ and $B_Q = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{(0.10)^3}$, so $\dfrac{B_P}{B_Q} = \dfrac{2 \times (0.10)^3}{(0.20)^3} = \dfrac{2}{8} = \dfrac{1}{4}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The field of a short bar magnet at an end-on point 30 cm from its centre is to be matched by its field at a broadside-on point. How far from the centre must the broadside-on point be, in cm (3 significant figures)?
questions.solution_md: Equal fields need $\dfrac{m}{d_b^3} = \dfrac{2m}{(30)^3}$, so $d_b^3 = \dfrac{(30)^3}{2} = 13500$ cm³ and $d_b = \dfrac{30}{2^{1/3}} = 23.8$ cm. The broadside-on point must be closer, because the broadside-on field is only half as strong at the same distance.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 1.6 A m² is held at 25° to a uniform magnetic field of 0.050 T. Find the torque on it, in mN m (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\tau = mB\sin\theta = 1.6 \times 0.050 \times \sin 25^\circ \approx 0.080 \times 0.4226 \approx 0.0338$ N m, i.e. $0.0338 \times 10^{3} = 33.8$ mN m.

questions.stem_md: A short magnet hung at 30° to a uniform field of 0.032 T experiences a torque of 0.012 N m. Find its magnetic moment, in A m².
questions.solution_md: $m = \dfrac{\tau}{B\sin\theta} = \dfrac{0.012}{0.032 \times 0.5} = 0.75$ A m².

marking_scheme.step: m = τ/(B sin θ) = 0.75 A m²

questions.stem_md: A short bar magnet of moment 0.40 A m² lies on a horizontal table with its north pole pointing geographic north. The horizontal component of the Earth’s field there is 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T, directed north. Find the distance from the centre of the magnet, in cm, of the points where the resultant horizontal field is zero (the neutral points).
questions.solution_md: With m pointing north, the magnet's field end-on is along m and adds to the Earth's field, but broadside-on it is opposite to m, i.e. southwards. So the neutral points lie on the east–west line through the centre, where $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{d^3} = B_H$: $d^3 = \dfrac{10^{-7} \times 0.40}{4.0 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m³, so $d = 0.10$ m, i.e. $0.10 \times 100 = 10$ cm, on each side of the magnet.

marking_scheme.step: Neutral points broadside-on (field opposite to m cancels B_H)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At equal large distances from a short bar magnet, the end-on field is twice as strong as the broadside-on field.

**Reason (R):** The field of a short bar magnet weakens as the inverse cube of the distance from its centre.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, but R does not explain A: the 1/d³ law holds equally in both positions; the factor 2 comes from the different geometry of the two positions (2m/d³ against m/d³) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A pivoted compass needle sits in a uniform magnetic field. Through what smallest angle from the field direction must it be turned for the torque on it to be half of the largest torque it can feel?
questions.solution_md: $\tau = mB\sin\theta$, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac12$ gives $\theta = 30^\circ$ (150° also works, on the far side) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet lies on a horizontal table with its magnetic moment pointing north. A uniform horizontal magnetic field pointing east is switched on. The torque on the magnet points

options.text_md: vertically upwards, so the magnet turns anticlockwise as seen from above
towards the east, along the field
towards the north, along the magnet
vertically downwards, so the magnet turns clockwise as seen from above

questions.solution_md: With x east, y north and z up, $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B \propto \hat y \times \hat x = -\hat z$: downwards. A torque pointing down turns the magnet clockwise as seen from above, swinging m from north towards east, into line with B — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Show that the formulae for the field of a bar magnet of magnetic length 2l reduce to (μ₀/4π)2m/d³ end-on and (μ₀/4π)m/d³ broadside-on when d ≫ l, and state the direction of the field in each position.

answer.model_answer_md: End-on: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2md}{(d^2 - l^2)^2}$; for $d \gg l$, $(d^2 - l^2)^2 \approx d^4$, so $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{d^3}$, **along m**. Broadside-on: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2}}$ and $(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2} \approx d^3$, so $B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{d^3}$, **opposite to m** (parallel to the axis, from the N end towards the S end).

questions.solution_md: Neglect l² beside d².

marking_scheme.step: Broadside-on limit m/d³, opposite to m

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of magnetic length 8.0 cm has a magnetic moment of 0.90 A m². Find the field at an end-on point 20 cm from its centre (a) with the formula for a magnet of finite length, (b) treating it as a short magnet. (c) By what percentage does the short-magnet value fall below the value in (a)?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $l = 0.040$ m, $d = 0.20$ m: $d^2 - l^2 = 0.04 - 0.0016 = 0.0384$ m². $B = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{2 \times 0.90 \times 0.20}{(0.0384)^2} \approx 2.44 \times 10^{-5}$ T.
(b) $B \approx 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{2 \times 0.90}{(0.20)^3} = 2.25 \times 10^{-5}$ T.
(c) $\dfrac{(a) - (b)}{(a)} \times 100 \approx 7.8$ per cent: the short-magnet formula is about 8% low because l is not negligible beside d.

questions.solution_md: Finite-length end-on formula, then 2m/d³.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet can turn freely about a vertical axis in a uniform horizontal field. In which two orientations is the torque on it zero? Which of them is stable, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: The torque mB sin θ is zero when the moment points **along** the field (θ = 0°) or **exactly against** it (θ = 180°). θ = 0° is **stable**: a small twist produces a torque that turns the magnet **back**. At θ = 180° a small twist produces a torque that turns it **further away**, so that position is **unstable**.

questions.solution_md: sin θ = 0 at 0° and 180°; restoring or not.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 2.0 A m² hangs from a thread so that it can turn in a horizontal plane, in a uniform horizontal field of 0.030 T. (a) Find the torque on it when its axis is perpendicular to the field. (b) At what angle from the field is the torque 0.030 N m? (c) The magnet is at rest along the field when the field is suddenly reversed. Describe and explain what happens.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\tau = mB = 2.0 \times 0.030 = 0.060$ N m.
(b) $\sin\theta = \dfrac{0.030}{0.060} = 0.5$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$ (or $150^\circ$).
(c) Now m points opposite to B: θ = 180°, where the torque is zero but the equilibrium is **unstable**. The slightest disturbance produces a torque that turns the magnet further, so it swings right round, overshoots and oscillates, and finally settles with m along the new field.

questions.solution_md: τ = mB sin θ; stability at 180°.

marking_scheme.step: Unstable at 180°: turns round to align with the reversed field

questions.stem_md: At a broadside-on point 20 cm from the centre of a short bar magnet, the field due to the magnet is 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ T. Find the magnetic moment of the magnet, in A m².
A rectangular loop 15 cm × 8.0 cm lies flat on a horizontal bench in a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T that is directed at 30° above the horizontal. Find the magnetic flux through the loop, in mWb.
questions.solution_md: The normal to the loop is vertical, so it makes $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ with $\vec B$. $A = 0.15 \times 0.080 = 0.012$ m². $\Phi = BA\cos 60^\circ = 0.25 \times 0.012 \times 0.5 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, i.e. $1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 1.5$ mWb.

questions.stem_md: An old reference book gives the strength of the Earth’s magnetic field at a place in Bhopal as 0.46 gauss. Expressed in tesla, this is
questions.solution_md: 1 G $= 10^{-4}$ T, so the field is $0.46 \times 10^{-4} = 4.6 \times 10^{-5}$ T — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Magnetic flux is flux density times area, so a flux density of one tesla through one square metre held normal to the field gives a flux of one ___.
questions.solution_md: One **weber** (1 Wb = 1 T m²).

questions.stem_md: As a flat coil is turned in a uniform magnetic field, the largest flux through it is 3.6 × 10⁻³ Wb. Find the flux, in mWb, when the plane of the coil makes 30° with the field.
questions.solution_md: The plane at $30^\circ$ to the field means the normal is at $\theta = 60^\circ$. $\Phi = \Phi_\text{max}\cos\theta = 3.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.5 = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, i.e. $1.8 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 1.8$ mWb.

questions.stem_md: A hemispherical bowl of radius R rests with its rim horizontal in a uniform vertical magnetic field B. The magnetic flux through its curved surface has magnitude

options.text_md: 2πR²B, since the curved area is 2πR²
zero, since the field lines enter and leave the bowl
πR²B, the same as through the flat circle of the rim
4πR²B, the area of a whole sphere times B

questions.solution_md: The bowl and the flat disc of its rim together form a closed surface, through which the net magnetic flux is zero. So every line that crosses the disc also crosses the curved surface: flux $= \pi R^2B$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A magnetic flux of 4.8 × 10⁻⁴ Wb passes normally through a flat area of 60 cm². Find the flux density, in gauss.

**Assertion (A):** Magnetic flux through a surface is a scalar quantity, although the flux density B is a vector.

**Reason (R):** Flux is the scalar (dot) product of $\vec B$ with the area vector of the surface: $\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: a dot product of two vectors is a scalar — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Since one tesla equals one weber per square metre, a field of one gauss can also be written as 10⁻⁴ Wb m⁻².

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T and 1 T = 1 Wb m⁻², so 1 G = 10⁻⁴ Wb m⁻².

questions.stem_md: Define magnetic flux through a plane surface and state its SI unit. A flat coil is turned in a uniform field: in which orientations is the flux through it (i) greatest, (ii) zero?

answer.model_answer_md: Magnetic flux $\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A = BA\cos\theta$, where θ is the angle between B and the **normal** to the surface; SI unit the **weber** (1 Wb = 1 T m²). (i) Greatest, $BA$, when the plane of the coil is **perpendicular** to the field. (ii) Zero when the plane of the coil is **parallel** to the field.

questions.solution_md: Φ = BA cos θ.

marking_scheme.step: Greatest with plane ⟂ B; zero with plane ∥ B

questions.stem_md: A circular coil of radius 7.0 cm lies in a uniform magnetic field of 0.12 T. Find the flux through one turn when (a) its plane is perpendicular to the field, (b) its normal makes 37° with the field, (c) its plane is parallel to the field. Also express the field in gauss.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.070)^2 \approx 0.0154$ m², so $\Phi = BA \approx 0.12 \times 0.0154 \approx 1.85 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb.
(b) $\Phi = BA\cos 37^\circ \approx 1.85 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.799 \approx 1.48 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb.
(c) No field lines cross the coil: $\Phi = 0$. The field is $0.12 \times 10^{4} = 1200$ G.

questions.solution_md: Φ = BA cos θ; 1 T = 10⁴ G.

questions.stem_md: An iron rod 12 cm long with a cross-section of 0.50 cm² is magnetised until its magnetic moment is 4.2 A m². Find its magnetisation, in units of 10⁵ A m⁻¹.
A magnetic intensity of 2.4 × 10³ A m⁻¹ magnetises a crystal of a paramagnetic salt to 1.8 A m⁻¹. Find the susceptibility of the salt, in units of 10⁻⁴.
questions.solution_md: $\chi = \dfrac{M}{H} = \dfrac{1.8}{2.4 \times 10^{3}} = 7.5 \times 10^{-4}$, i.e. $7.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{4} = 7.5$ (small and positive, as for a paramagnet).

questions.stem_md: A paramagnetic salt has a susceptibility of 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ at 250 K. Assuming Curie’s law, find its susceptibility at 77 °C, in units of 10⁻⁴.
questions.solution_md: 77 °C is $77 + 273 = 350$ K. By Curie's law $\chi T$ is constant, so $\chi_2 = 4.2 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{250}{350} = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}$, i.e. $3.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{4} = 3.0$.

questions.stem_md: In a soft-iron sample the magnetic intensity is 500 A m⁻¹ and the magnetic field is 1.4 T. Find the susceptibility of the iron (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $B = \mu_0(H + M)$, so $M = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0} - H \approx \dfrac{1.4}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} - 500 \approx 1.114 \times 10^{6}$ A m$^{-1}$. Then $\chi = \dfrac{M}{H} \approx 2227$, i.e. $\chi = 2230$ to 3 significant figures: a ferromagnet.

questions.stem_md: A sample has a relative permeability of 0.99990. Its magnetic susceptibility, and the class of material it belongs to, are

options.text_md: +1.0 × 10⁻⁴; paramagnetic
0.99990; paramagnetic
−0.99990; diamagnetic
−1.0 × 10⁻⁴; diamagnetic

questions.solution_md: $\chi = \mu_r - 1 = 0.99990 - 1 = -1.0 \times 10^{-4}$: small and negative, so the material is diamagnetic — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A small sphere of a material whose susceptibility is −1.6 × 10⁻⁵ is placed in a uniform magnetic field. Compared with the empty space around it, the field lines inside the sphere are

options.text_md: very slightly more crowded, because the material is paramagnetic
much more crowded, because the material is ferromagnetic
absent, because the field is completely expelled
very slightly less crowded, because the material is diamagnetic

questions.solution_md: A small negative χ marks a diamagnet: its magnetisation opposes H, so B inside is very slightly smaller and the lines spread out a little — option (d). Complete expulsion happens only in a superconductor (χ = −1).

questions.stem_md: Gadolinium has a Curie temperature of about 293 K (20 °C). A gadolinium bar is tested with a strong magnet on a winter morning at 10 °C and again on a summer afternoon at 35 °C. The bar is

options.text_md: ferromagnetic in the morning but only paramagnetic in the afternoon
paramagnetic in the morning but ferromagnetic in the afternoon
ferromagnetic on both occasions
diamagnetic on both occasions

questions.solution_md: 10 °C = 283 K is below the Curie temperature, so the domains survive and the bar is ferromagnetic. 35 °C = 308 K is above it, so the bar is only paramagnetic — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A paramagnetic sample is cooled from 300 K to 100 K while the applied magnetic intensity is held fixed (well below saturation). Its magnetisation

options.text_md: becomes about one third as large
becomes about three times as large
stays the same
becomes about nine times as large

questions.solution_md: M = χH with χ = C/T. At fixed H, M ∝ 1/T, so reducing T to one third triples M — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When a weak magnetic field is first applied to an unmagnetised piece of soft iron, its magnetisation grows mainly because

options.text_md: each atom acquires a new magnetic moment opposite to the field
the iron warms up, so its atoms vibrate less
the electrons stop moving in their orbits
domains already magnetised roughly along the field grow at the expense of their neighbours

questions.solution_md: In weak fields the domain walls shift, so favourably oriented domains enlarge. In stronger fields whole domains rotate towards the field, until the sample saturates — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity describing a magnetised steel bar (Column A) with its SI unit (Column B).

options.text_md: Magnetic flux through its cross-section
Magnetic field B inside it
Its magnetic moment
Its magnetisation M

questions.solution_md: Flux → weber (1 → s); field B → tesla (2 → q); magnetic moment → A m² (3 → p); magnetisation → A m⁻¹ (4 → r).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The susceptibility of a paramagnetic salt rises when the salt is cooled.

**Reason (R):** At lower temperatures thermal agitation upsets the alignment of the permanent atomic magnetic moments less.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the field lines up the permanent moments more effectively when thermal agitation is weaker, so χ = C/T rises — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Iron heated above its Curie temperature (about 1043 K) can no longer hold any permanent magnetisation.

**Reason (R):** Above its Curie temperature iron becomes diamagnetic.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: thermal agitation destroys the alignment within the domains. R is false: iron becomes paramagnetic, not diamagnetic — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Three samples X, Y and Z have susceptibilities −2.3 × 10⁻⁵, +6.0 × 10⁻⁴ and +2.0 × 10³. Classify each, and say which is pushed out of, and which is most strongly pulled into, the strong-field region near a magnet pole.

answer.model_answer_md: X: small negative χ, so **diamagnetic**. Y: small positive χ, so **paramagnetic**. Z: very large positive χ, so **ferromagnetic**. X is **pushed weakly towards the weaker field**, away from the pole; Z is **pulled in most strongly**, while Y is attracted only feebly.

questions.solution_md: Classify by sign and size of χ.

marking_scheme.step: X dia, Y para, Z ferro
X pushed out; Z pulled in most strongly

questions.stem_md: A paramagnetic salt in a fixed magnetising field is warmed from 200 K to 400 K. By what factor does its magnetisation change? Explain in terms of its atomic magnetic moments.

answer.model_answer_md: By Curie’s law χ = C/T, so at fixed H, **M = χH ∝ 1/T**: doubling T **halves** M (factor 0.5). The atoms carry **permanent moments** that the field tries to line up; stronger **thermal agitation** at the higher temperature disorders them more, so fewer point along the field.

questions.solution_md: M ∝ 1/T at fixed H.

marking_scheme.step: Thermal agitation disorders the permanent moments

questions.stem_md: A long solenoid with 1200 turns per metre carries a current of 0.75 A and is wound on a core of relative permeability 850. Calculate (a) the magnetic intensity H, (b) the magnetic field B in the core, (c) the magnetisation M of the core.
questions.solution_md: H = nI; B = μ₀μrH; M = χH.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of the magnetisation M, the magnetic intensity H and the susceptibility χ of a sample placed in a solenoid. Use B = μ₀(H + M) to show that μr = 1 + χ, and hence find the relative permeability of copper, whose susceptibility is −9.6 × 10⁻⁶.

answer.model_answer_md: **M** is the net magnetic moment per unit volume of the sample; **H** is the magnetic intensity due to the current in the solenoid ($nI$); both in A m$^{-1}$. **χ** = M/H, a pure number. With $M = \chi H$, $B = \mu_0(H + \chi H) = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H$; comparing with $B = \mu_0\mu_rH$ gives $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$. For copper $\mu_r = 1 - 0.0000096 = 0.9999904$, just below 1: diamagnetic.

questions.solution_md: Substitute M = χH.

questions.stem_md: Using the behaviour of atomic magnetic moments, explain why (a) every material shows some diamagnetism, (b) the susceptibility of a paramagnet depends on temperature while that of a diamagnet hardly does, (c) a ferromagnet can have a susceptibility of several thousand.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) An applied field alters the **orbital motion** of electrons in every atom, **inducing** small moments that **oppose** it; this is masked when permanent moments exist. (b) Paramagnetism comes from **aligning permanent moments**, which **thermal agitation** disorders, so χ = C/T; induced moments need no alignment, so diamagnetic χ is nearly **independent of T**. (c) In a ferromagnet neighbouring moments line up **spontaneously in domains**; a modest field merely **reorients whole domains**, giving a huge M for a small H.

questions.solution_md: Induced versus permanent moments; domains.

marking_scheme.step: Induced opposing moments in all atoms
Thermal agitation affects alignment of permanent moments only
Domains reoriented: huge M for small H

questions.stem_md: A long solenoid with 2000 turns per metre carries 0.60 A and is filled with a paramagnetic liquid of susceptibility 3.5 × 10⁻³. Find the magnetisation of the liquid, in A m⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: H = 1200 A m⁻¹ and M = χH = 4.2 A m⁻¹

questions.stem_md: An electromagnet is a coil wound on a soft-iron core and is used well below saturation. Which one of these changes would NOT make its field stronger?

options.text_md: increasing the current in the coil
rewinding the same number of turns with thicker wire, the current being kept the same
winding more turns on the same length of core
replacing the core with one of higher relative permeability

questions.solution_md: B ≈ μ₀μr nI depends on the turns per unit length, the current and the permeability of the core, not on the thickness of the wire once n and I are fixed — option (b). (Thicker wire only lets a larger current flow from the same supply.)

questions.stem_md: The magnet of a moving-coil loudspeaker must keep its magnetisation for many years, despite vibration and the changing field of the voice coil beside it. Its material should have

options.text_md: high retentivity and high coercivity
high retentivity and low coercivity
low retentivity and low coercivity
a susceptibility that is small and negative

questions.solution_md: High retentivity leaves a strong field after magnetisation; high coercivity means a large reverse field is needed to destroy it, so stray fields and knocks do not demagnetise it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For the core of a 230 V, 50 Hz mains transformer, which kind of B–H loop is best?

options.text_md: a tall, narrow loop: high permeability, low coercivity and a small loop area
a wide loop with a large area: high coercivity
a loop that never saturates, with coercivity as high as possible
no loop at all: a diamagnetic core

questions.solution_md: The core is taken round its loop 50 times a second; the energy lost each cycle grows with the loop area, so a narrow loop (low coercivity) keeps the core cool, and high permeability gives a large flux for a small current — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After a ferromagnetic sample has been magnetised to saturation, the reverse magnetic intensity needed to bring its flux density back to zero is called its

options.text_md: coercivity
retentivity
susceptibility
saturation magnetisation

questions.solution_md: The **coercivity** is the reverse H that reduces B to zero; the retentivity is the B left when H is reduced to zero — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On the B–H loop of a ferromagnet, the flux density that remains when the magnetising field H has been brought back to zero after saturation is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The **retentivity** (also called remanence or residual magnetism).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Steel rather than soft iron is chosen for making permanent magnets.

**Reason (R):** Steel has a much higher coercivity than soft iron, so its magnetisation is not easily destroyed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: a permanent magnet must resist demagnetisation by knocks and stray fields, which needs a high coercivity — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A material with a large coercivity and a wide B–H loop is a good choice for the core of a transformer.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A wide loop means a large energy loss as heat in every cycle; transformer cores need a narrow loop (low coercivity) and high permeability, e.g. soft iron or silicon steel.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons, linked to the B–H loop, why transformer cores are made of soft iron (or silicon steel) and not of hard steel.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Soft iron has a **low coercivity**, so its B–H loop is **narrow** and little energy is lost as heat in each of the 50 cycles every second (**small hysteresis loss**). (ii) It has a **high permeability**, so a small magnetising current produces a **large flux** linking both coils. Hard steel has a wide loop and would overheat.

questions.solution_md: Narrow loop; high permeability.

marking_scheme.step: Low coercivity, narrow loop: small hysteresis loss
High permeability: large flux for small current

questions.stem_md: Two ferromagnetic samples are tested. P has a retentivity of 1.2 T and a coercivity of 50 A m⁻¹; Q has a retentivity of 0.90 T and a coercivity of 4.5 × 10⁴ A m⁻¹. Which would you use for a permanent magnet and which for the core of an electromagnet? Justify your choice.

answer.model_answer_md: **Q for the permanent magnet**: its very large coercivity means stray fields and knocks cannot easily demagnetise it, and 0.90 T retentivity is ample. **P for the electromagnet core**: its tiny coercivity lets it lose its magnetism as soon as the current is switched off, despite its higher retentivity.

questions.solution_md: Coercivity decides.

marking_scheme.step: Q for the permanent magnet (high coercivity)

questions.stem_md: An electromagnet made by winding a coil on a soft-iron rod is too weak to lift a load. Suggest three changes that would make it stronger, and explain why raising the current further eventually stops helping.

answer.model_answer_md: The field in the core is about μ₀μr nI, so: (i) wind **more turns per unit length**; (ii) pass a **larger current**; (iii) use a core of **higher permeability**, or bend it into a **U shape** so that both poles act on the load across a small air gap. Raising I helps only until the core **saturates**: once nearly all its **domains are aligned**, M cannot grow, so B rises only by the small μ₀H of the coil itself.

questions.solution_md: B ≈ μ₀μr nI up to saturation.

marking_scheme.step: Two of: more n, more I, higher μr
Third valid change (U shape, small gap, etc.)

questions.stem_md: Describe the B–H loop obtained when a ferromagnetic sample is taken through a complete cycle of magnetisation, and explain what is meant by saturation, retentivity and coercivity on it. (Describe the sketch in words.)

answer.model_answer_md: From the unmagnetised state, B rises along a curve as H increases until it levels off at **saturation**, when nearly all the domains are aligned. When H is reduced to zero, B does not return to zero: the value left is the **retentivity**. A reverse H, the **coercivity**, is needed to make B zero. Continuing to large negative H saturates the sample the other way, and bringing H back round closes the loop: B always **lags** behind H.

questions.solution_md: Saturation, retentivity, coercivity on the loop.

marking_scheme.step: Shape: rises to saturation, loop closed through reverse saturation

questions.stem_md: An air-cored solenoid produces a field of 1.6 mT. A soft-iron core of relative permeability 700 is slid in, and the current is unchanged (the iron stays well below saturation). Find the new field in the core, in tesla.

A coil of 400 turns is wound uniformly along a soft-iron core 25 cm long, of relative permeability 900. What current is needed to produce a field of 1.2 T in the core? Give the answer in amperes (3 significant figures).

(a) Compare the field lines of a bar magnet with those of a current-carrying solenoid, and explain why magnetic field lines always form closed loops. [2] (b) A solenoid 30 cm long has 900 turns of radius 1.2 cm and carries 2.0 A. Find (i) its magnetic moment, (ii) the magnetic field near its centre, (iii) the magnetic flux through its cross-section there. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Outside, both give the same pattern: lines leave one end (N), curve round and enter the other end (S); inside, the lines run from S to N along the axis, so every line is a closed loop. The magnet behaves as an equivalent solenoid because its aligned atomic current loops act like the turns. Lines close because there are no magnetic monopoles: there is nothing for a line to start or end on.

(b)(i) $A = \pi(0.012)^2 \approx 4.52 \times 10^{-4}$ m²; $m = NIA = 900 \times 2.0 \times 4.52 \times 10^{-4} \approx 0.814$ A m².
(ii) $n = \dfrac{900}{0.30} = 3000$ m$^{-1}$; $B = \mu_0nI = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 3000 \times 2.0 \approx 7.54 \times 10^{-3}$ T.
(iii) $\Phi = BA \approx 7.54 \times 10^{-3} \times 4.52 \times 10^{-4} \approx 3.41 \times 10^{-6}$ Wb.

questions.solution_md: Same pattern; no monopoles; m = NIA, B = μ₀nI, Φ = BA.

marking_scheme.step: Same pattern; S → N inside, closed loops

questions.stem_md: (a) Write the expressions for the magnetic field of a bar magnet of magnetic length 2l and moment m at a point a distance d from its centre (i) end-on, (ii) broadside-on, and state the direction of the field in each position. [2] (b) A bar magnet of magnetic length 6.0 cm has a moment of 0.75 A m². Find the field at a broadside-on point 4.0 cm from its centre. [2] (c) A small compass needle of moment 0.020 A m² is held at that point with its axis perpendicular to the field there. Find the torque on it. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a)(i) $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2md}{(d^2 - l^2)^2}$, along m (from the S end towards the N end). (ii) $B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2}}$, opposite to m, parallel to the axis of the magnet.

(b) $l = 0.030$ m, $d = 0.040$ m: $d^2 + l^2 = 0.0016 + 0.0009 = 0.0025$ m², so $(d^2 + l^2)^{3/2} = (0.050)^3 = 1.25 \times 10^{-4}$ m³. $B = 10^{-7} \times \dfrac{0.75}{1.25 \times 10^{-4}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-4}$ T.

(c) $\tau = mB\sin 90^\circ = 0.020 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-4} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ N m.

questions.solution_md: Formulae; broadside-on value; τ = mB.

questions.stem_md: (a) Define the relative permeability and the susceptibility of a material, and state how each identifies a ferromagnetic material. [1] (b) A Rowland ring (an iron toroid) has a mean radius of 10 cm and is wound uniformly with 500 turns carrying 0.40 A. The field measured in the iron is 0.60 T. Find (i) the magnetic intensity H, (ii) the relative permeability of the iron, (iii) its susceptibility and magnetisation. [3] (c) State what would happen to the relative permeability if the ring were heated above 1043 K. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\mu_r = \mu/\mu_0 = B/\mu_0H$; $\chi = M/H = \mu_r - 1$. For a ferromagnet both are very large (hundreds to thousands).

(b)(i) $H = \dfrac{NI}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{500 \times 0.40}{2\pi \times 0.10} \approx 318$ A m$^{-1}$.
(ii) $\mu_0H = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 318.3 \approx 4.0 \times 10^{-4}$ T, so $\mu_r = \dfrac{0.60}{4.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 1500$.
(iii) $\chi = \mu_r - 1 = 1499$; $M = \chi H \approx 1499 \times 318 \approx 4.77 \times 10^{5}$ A m$^{-1}$.

(c) 1043 K is the Curie temperature of iron: above it the domains break up, the iron becomes paramagnetic and $\mu_r$ falls to just above 1.

questions.solution_md: H = NI/2πr; μr = B/μ₀H; χ = μr − 1; Curie temperature.

marking_scheme.step: Definitions; both very large for a ferromagnet

questions.stem_md: (a) Distinguish diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic substances by the sign and size of their susceptibility and relative permeability, giving one example of each. [2] (b) State Curie’s law and explain why paramagnetic susceptibility depends on temperature. [1] (c) A paramagnetic salt has a susceptibility of 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ at 150 K. Find its Curie constant, and the temperature at which its susceptibility is 2.1 × 10⁻⁴. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diamagnetic:** χ small and negative (about $-10^{-5}$), $\mu_r$ slightly below 1, e.g. bismuth. **Paramagnetic:** χ small and positive ($10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$), $\mu_r$ slightly above 1, e.g. aluminium. **Ferromagnetic:** χ and $\mu_r$ very large (hundreds to thousands), e.g. iron.

(b) $\chi = C/T$: the susceptibility of a paramagnet is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature, because thermal agitation disorders the permanent atomic moments that the field tries to align.

(c) $C = \chi T = 6.3 \times 10^{-4} \times 150 = 0.0945$ K. $T = \dfrac{C}{\chi} = \dfrac{0.0945}{2.1 \times 10^{-4}} = 450$ K.

questions.solution_md: Classes; χ = C/T.

marking_scheme.step: Sign and size of χ, μr for the three classes

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, as you would draw it, a labelled B–H loop for a ferromagnetic material, marking the retentivity and the coercivity. [2] (b) The loops of soft iron and of steel are compared. State two differences between them. [1] (c) Name, with a reason, a suitable material for (i) the core of the electromagnet in an electric bell, (ii) the magnet of a moving-coil galvanometer, (iii) the core of a step-down transformer. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Axes H (horizontal) and B (vertical). From the origin B rises along a curve to saturation. As H is reduced to zero, B falls only to a positive value, the **retentivity** (intercept on the B axis). A reverse H, the **coercivity** (intercept on the negative H axis), brings B to zero; B then saturates in the reverse direction, and increasing H again closes the loop through the negative retentivity and the positive coercivity.

(b) Soft iron gives a **narrower** loop with a much **smaller coercivity** and a **smaller area** (less energy lost per cycle); its retentivity and permeability are slightly larger than those of steel.

(c)(i) **Soft iron**: high permeability, low coercivity, so the armature is released as soon as the current breaks. (ii) A hard material such as **steel or alnico**: high retentivity and high coercivity, so the magnet stays strong. (iii) **Laminated soft iron or silicon steel**: narrow loop for small hysteresis loss and high permeability.

questions.solution_md: Loop features; soft against hard; choice by property.

marking_scheme.step: Two differences: narrower loop, smaller coercivity and area for soft iron
Bell: soft iron; galvanometer: steel or alnico
Transformer: laminated soft iron or silicon steel, with reasons
